The letter of Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, on the book concerning the praises of the most holy Anne. To the venerable and most religious father, Lord Rumuld Laupach, prior of the convent of Frankfurt, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel: Johannes of Trittenheim, Abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin in Sponheim, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, sends greeting and charity.

Desiring to satisfy our vow and your requests, excellent father, we have written with sincere devotion a book on the praises of the most holy Mother Anne, and have dedicated it to your name, since before others you seemed worthy to us, as being a very great worshipper and most devout lover of the same venerable Anne.

But from the history about her which is rather widely circulated we have taken little or nothing, because it seemed to us both less well proven and, in very many places, apocryphal. Yet we did not wish to refute those accounts, lest we give simple people an occasion for murmuring, if, as they themselves think, we were to censure with new presumption things approved by antiquity. We have therefore left that history untouched, and whatever had been known as most fitting by faith, truth, and reason, we have brought together by God’s gift for the honor of holy Mother Anne.

We have also excluded the miracles of Saint Anne from this volume, lest we make our treatise suspect to learned men, who do not easily give credence to such things. And so at another time, if you wish, a history of them will be composed. If you should happen to hesitate over anything, write back; you will find us ready to show you and everyone the reason for each of the things we have written. After the end of this work we have added certain poems on the praises of the holy Mother, which have been sent to us by various learned men. Farewell.
From Sponheim, on the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord 1494.
Here begins the treatise of Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, on the praises of the venerable and most blessed Anne, mother of the Mother of God.

Necessity compels me, and devotion of mind urges me, to write, according to the powers of my ability, for the edification of the faithful, the praises of the most blessed Anne, mother of the Mother of God, and to declare in truthful narration how greatly she has been accustomed in her kindness to aid the wretched. But when I consider the poverty of my understanding, impure as I am, I am afraid to speak of the most holy woman.

For how worthy of praise is she who bore the Mother of God? What speech will explain it? And so I wish to fashion something in honor of so great a mother, and I am afraid, because whatever I say is less than her praises; whatever I write is far beneath the majesty of the matter. Yet when I recall to memory her benefits toward the wretched, I cannot keep silent from her praises, even if I wish. Therefore her very great kindness has deserved the fulfillment of my vow, has stirred up devotion, and requires the display of honor. The devout, and, not to call it importunate, petition of my friends has no less driven me to dare this; from their faith and prayer our weakness has received confidence. Although, then, I know myself to be a sinner, although I am not sufficient to praise worthily the most holy parent of the Queen of heaven, nevertheless I ought by no means to withdraw from the praise I have undertaken, lest I seem to incur the fault of ingratitude.

I shall attempt, according to my devotion, what I can, because no one is required by God to do what he cannot. No one is judged empty of good will before the eternal judge. Therefore I, a man, will praise the lady; a servant, the mistress; a sinner, the most holy one. For he did not restrain sinners from the praise of God who said in the psalm: “Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples.” Truly, when he summons the nations to the praise of the Lord, what else does he call but sinners? For they were far from righteousness, because they worshiped not God but idols. Therefore no one is permitted to keep silent from the praises of God, since even idolatrous nations are called to repentance. Let all, then, praise the Lord who receive his mercy; let all who live in the flesh praise him, because he himself is the one who made us all, he himself who gives life. Let the righteous and sinner alike praise: the one because he has been preserved by the mercy of the Lord so that he did not fall, the other because, even after his fall, he has been raised up so that he might not perish forever. And although praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner, still no one is excused from the praises of God by a guilty conscience, since by his mercy all are preserved for repentance. Let the righteous bring praise, the sinner confession. Let the former praise because, by preserving grace, he stood firm; and let the latter confess because, by mercy following after, he rose again. “Praise the Lord, O my soul; I shall praise my God in my life; I shall sing to the Lord as long as I shall be.” I shall open my mouth to confess the Lord; I shall likewise ready my mind and my pen.
I shall sing the praises of the most blessed mother Anne with what devotion I can.

For if we are commanded to praise God generally in his saints, we are without doubt urged to honor his parents more especially. For he who commanded us to honor our own parents certainly does not exclude his own according to the flesh. Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, it is holy to offer diligent praises of devotion to those from whose blood we believe the flesh of the Son of God was taken. Among them the most blessed Mother of God rightly holds first place, whose merits of holiness are so great that she has been exalted in heaven above the choirs of angels.

After her comes that most holy mother Anne, of whom we have undertaken to speak; just as in the flesh she is nearest to the Son of God, so in life and merits she is believed to be acceptable before the other saints. Nor may we doubt her holiness, since we believe that she gave birth to the Mother of God without the stain of original sin. For she could not have been the mother of so great a Virgin unless she was holy, through whose virginal childbearing we received the remedies of eternal salvation.

Anne is the holy root; Mary the Virgin is the most holy tree; the Son of God is the fruit, the medicine of souls. A good tree, a holy tree, a tree most fruitful without human cultivation, which took its beginning from a holy root and its growth from the richness of the heavenly rain. A good root never brings forth a bad tree, nor does a good tree bear bad fruits. A good tree cannot stand without a root, nor can good fruits be borne unless the tree is good. As a tree is known by its fruit, so what sort the mother is is made clear in the daughter.

In the most holy Mother of God we understand what we ought to think concerning the holiness of her mother. A childbearing without the fault of original stain befitted none but a holy mother, one who would conceive and bear the Mother of God; it suited none but one most pleasing to God and, beyond all then living in Israel, devout. The first instruction of the daughter shows how Anne loved God above all things. The little child is read to have been entrusted to the Lord; she is remembered to have served in the temple of God; she is believed to have been conceived without any fault and always to have lived holy in the world.

What more do you require? Is such an excellent life of the daughter from infancy not enough to declare the mother’s merits? If Anne had not been most holy, she would not have instructed her daughter so diligently and devoutly for the honor of God. We know that daughters are formed according to what their mothers are. But the most blessed mother Anne, just as she surpasses all women in merit and holiness, so she took care to instruct her daughter from childhood in the love of God more diligently than all the saints.

If, then, we love the Son of God, if we honor his most pure Mother, why do we grow lukewarm and fall silent in praise of his most holy grandmother and mother Anne? If we seek the honor of the highest King, why do we not love his parents? Whoever despises the offspring of an emperor does injury to the king. If we love Christ Jesus, the emperor of all, if we revere his divine majesty, it is fitting that we honor his venerable grandmother, from whose

We believe without doubt that he came forth from her daughter’s womb without the seed of man. Whatever praise and veneration we bestow on her, let us firmly believe that it belongs to the honor of the highest King. For the honor of the most holy mother Anne, all faithful, come together; pay praises to the most high Lord in her memory; rejoice with religious devotion out of reverence for her.

Believe me, for I have experienced many of her benefits: you will have her ready as an advocate in every tribulation, if you celebrate her memory with faithful devotion. Therefore she is to be honored by all, for at her merits the Son of God grants favors at her nod; her honorable name the court of the citizens above honors with the greatest reverence; the queen of heaven, the mother of God, regards her as her sweetest parent. Whoever chooses her as patroness, whoever perseveres devoutly in her service, shall be saved both now and forever. For the Son of God, who is accustomed to grant benefits to mortals through his beloved mother, cannot deny them to the merits of his grandmother; indeed, he sometimes grants greater things through her, so that he may draw us, as it were by gifts, to her memory, long neglected. The Son of God can never despise his own parents, he who so earnestly commanded us to honor the parents of others.
Invocation of the author to God and Saint Anne and all the saints above, that the grace of writing may be granted.

O God, true light, who enlightens every person coming into this world; God, who justifies the ungodly and calls sinners to repentance; God, who gives wisdom to little ones and makes eloquent the tongues of those who stammer: grant me, I beseech you, pardon for my sins; grant me the wisdom of your praise; grant me light, through which I may understand, know, and love you, and may burn so with love for most blessed Anne that I may worthily embrace her praises in this work.

O God, who brought forth water from the hardest rock for your thirsty people in the desert, soften the hardness of my heart, that I may be able to praise you with such devotion of mind in your saints, in the grandmother of your Son, in the parents of your Only-Begotten, that, through your mercy and her intercession, this little night-work of ours may serve for devotion not only for me, but also for all who read it.

O God, who opened the mouth of the beast, so that it uttered human words against the foolish man, mercifully water the dryness of my tongue by the infusion of your grace. Strengthen my trembling hand with the Holy Spirit, that concerning most holy Anne I may write nothing except what is right, persuade nothing except what is holy, utter nothing except what is fitting. Grant me, I ask, almighty and eternal God, the help of heavenly grace in this work, you who have granted me the intention to undertake it. For I am a worm and not a man, wretched and unhappy, sold under my sin.

I who am not worthy to lift my face to heaven because of the multitude of my iniquity, much less to dare touch with impure lips the praises of most blessed Anne. But by your grace I am what I am, and all the good that I will and can do is yours. For you, Lord, enlighten the will by your grace, so that it may will good and be good; you also are he who grants us to work according to a good will. In all things we acknowledge your grace going before our will; in the good things we will and do, we proclaim your gifts without any merits of our own. Nothing comes from us but evil; nothing comes from you but good.

Since, therefore, I can do no good of myself without your grace, I devoutly flee to you; with humble subjection I call upon you, that what my merits hinder, you may mercifully bestow by your grace. Give me, Lord, wisdom, the attendant of your throne, that she may be with me and labor with me at all times, and especially in this work, in which with slender powers I have resolved to praise your name in holy mother Anne.

You also, Anne, most holy mother, whose memory I am treating, deign with your accustomed kindness to be present with me, that I may be made fit to describe your praises and, by your merits, be found a faithful proclaimer. My lady, my hope, my advocate in every tribulation, be graciously present now to me as I long to praise you; and you who by many benefits have stirred my will to write, obtain by your merits ability for my poor talent, so that it may be able to praise you worthily. I seek nothing except the honor of the three; I desire nothing except to please you; I intend to write nothing about your praises except what is right and true. Now, I pray, bring help; give the hand of assistance; obtain grace.

You also, immaculate Mother of God, who taught your servants to honor Anne, your venerable mother, be present with your merits to me as I long to describe her praises, so that the devotion of your servant may obtain in the work the due effect which the grace of God conceived in the mind. You also, blessed spirits of the heavenly fatherland, who rejoice in the most sacred fruit of the mother and the virgin daughter, our Lord Jesus Christ, by your prayers make me worthy to praise Anne, and obtain for me the grace of the Holy Spirit. If you honor mother and daughter in heavenly joy, it is fitting that you assist their praisers in this pilgrimage.

You also, devout worshipers of most blessed Anne, do not detract from my pious studies, but if in anything through weakness I have failed, excuse it through charity. Nothing is written by me through contention or empty glory; nothing of apocryphal uncertainty is alleged; nothing is taken up except what has been proved. I receive nothing that resists the divine Scriptures; I write nothing that stains the Christian faith; I introduce nothing that does not agree with holy things.

Therefore let no one more learned than I detract from me because I have praised you, Anne; let no equal disparage me; let no inferior insult me. What is true prevails, and what proceeds from truth does not fail. Let no one think me contemptible because I write about the most holy woman; let no one disturb my devotion; let no one mutter against the praises of lady mother Anne. I do not fear the barking of dogs; I do not dread the judgments of the unskilled; I do not shudder at the torches of envy. For I write for the devout, not for the wicked; for the studious, not for the ignorant; for the humble, not for the proud. May this present work please those for whom it is written; may it profit those to whom it is offered; may it serve those to whom it is presented. What have I to do with those who are outside? What is it to me if they do not think rightly? What is it to me if they gnaw at holy things beyond reason? I do not fear displeasing those whose rash judgments and censures I know.
A general exhortation to all the faithful, that the memory and feast of most holy Anne be venerated.

Hear me, you who love what is good and seek the Lord. I act as envoy; I am led by devotion; I am driven by charity. The mother of the Mother of God has sent me to proclaim her most holy merits. And now I come to you not with lofty speech, but as a simple man to the simple, a devout man to the devout. If you are Christians, if you are good, if you love the grace of the Lord’s incarnation, why do you not love his servants, that is, his parents? For they are the ones from whom the Son of God was born according to the flesh; and if their life had not been most holy, it would by no means have been so acceptable to God. But when he willed that his only-begotten Son should be born from them, he plainly showed how holy and dear to him they were. Among these, one shone forth before all others as most pleasing to God: Mary, the ever-virgin, chosen as the mother of that unique birth; and Joachim and most blessed Anne begot her without stain and brought her up most chastely in the fear of the Lord. The Son of this most sacred virgin is God, who redeemed us by his most holy passion. If you love the daughter, why do you not honor her mother? Had there been no mother, you would not have had the daughter.

Therefore my discourse now turns to you who dwell in the valley of tears and bitterness. I address you, sons of Adam, exiled from your homeland; I write to you who have been redeemed by the precious blood of the Son of God. I address you, I admonish and exhort you: if you love the Son of God, devoutly honor his kinsfolk according to the flesh. Among them, after his most holy Mother, divine mother Anne is set before you as the first of all to be honored; her holy merits are shown every day to the human race by very many miracles. Take her as your patron; celebrate her memory with greater devotion.

If you wish to please God, the supreme ruler, believe me, brothers, for I am going to speak the truth: if you love and honor the venerable mother with all your heart, you will learn by experience how much the heavenly emperor grants to her. She has such power with God that whatever she asks of him she is able to obtain without delay. Just as the heavenly King is believed to honor his mother before all others, so after her he venerates mother Anne before all the saints. And very often Anne commands for her faithful servants what her daughter refuses, not because that daughter does not know how to yield to petitions, but so that, in deference to the mother, she may be seen to stir us up to veneration of her. So too the supreme emperor is bent to mercy by the prayers of the saints, not because he begins to will what he did not will before, but so that, in showing regard for his elect, he may instruct us to honor them. For God is not moved in the manner of men, nor is he driven to anger by any disturbance; rather, always unchanging, he wills what he wills. And when he shows mercy at the prayers of the saints, he does not change his counsel, but mitigates his sentence.

Therefore, to obtain the mercy of God, for which our own merits are not sufficient, the suffrages of the saints must be implored for us, so that what we cannot attain by our own merits we may gain by their prayers. Now all the citizens of the heavenly homeland, even if they differ according to the quality of their merits, are nevertheless believed to be of one mind in act and will in helping our wretchedness, according to the variety of those who make supplication, if devotion asks it. For when the faith of the petitioner is aided by the merit of the advocate, it becomes doubled for obtaining what is sought. We can assess this not by conjecture but by experience, when we wonder that one person is heard and another disregarded by the saints. Two blind men come to make supplication to the merit of some saint: one is given sight; the other is left in his blindness. No contempt on the saint’s part is believed to be present; rather, the petitioner’s lack of trust is exposed. Without faith, devotion merits nothing.

I have set these things forth with sure consideration, so that if anyone should feel that most blessed Anne is not present to him with such readiness as we promise, he should not accuse us of falsehood, but recognize his own culpable lack of trust. For the greatest confidence before God and the saints is steadfast faith in their help. Moreover, no Christian doubts that those who are more excellent in merits have greater power with God. Therefore the most blessed Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary, as she surpasses all the saints in merits and holiness, so by right she is believed to surpass them all in power and majesty, as queen of heaven. At her right hand, if I may speak thus, we believe that most blessed mother Anne stands, whose life we know to have been most holy. There was no other woman holier than she in Israel, who in the conception of the Mother of God prepared a vessel without stain for the Holy Spirit. Finally, if Elizabeth, the mother of the Lord’s forerunner, is believed to have been filled with the Holy Spirit and with ineffable joy, let it be considered with how great exultation, joy, and grace the most holy mother of God’s parent ought to have been filled. As much as a king differs from a soldier, so in her own manner does Anne [unclear].

The merits of Lady Elizabeth are rightly set forth; Saint Elizabeth bore a soldier, Anne bore the Mother of God. There is no comparison where there is no likeness. If Elizabeth was full of grace because of John, I believe Anne obtained grace much more because of Mary.

Anne was holy before she conceived the Mother of God, yet in that conception she was sanctified still more abundantly, because she deserved to become the tabernacle of her who was full of grace above all creatures. We call a casket or ark in which the pledges of the saints are kept sanctified and honorable; how much more ought we to venerate Anne as venerable, honored, and sanctified, in whom the Mother of God lay without stain. Truly holy is she who bore her without the guilt of original stain, than whom no one was ever holier. Truly holy is she who was chosen to be the mother of the God-bearer before she was born.

O womb never to be named without honor, in which the ark of God deserved to be fashioned without stain. Blessed the belly that carried the Lady of heaven; happy the breasts that deserved to nurse the Mother of God. Run, peoples, from every side, and receive the blessing from the merits of your holy patroness.

For indeed, if the holy devotion of the faithful is directed toward her, we believe that through her the Almighty will give great gifts to mortals, and no smaller ones than he is accustomed to give through her daughter. Therefore you, faithful peoples, who believe the daughter of Saint Anne to be the Mother of God, who rest under the sanctified shadow of both, if you desire to please in the love of God, if you wish to come to the heavenly homeland, do not neglect the memory of this most holy mother. For after the Queen she is most powerful in the court of the heavenly Emperor, because from her blood the Son of God took flesh from the Virgin.

When in tribulation you cry to her, you will find help. She is rich enough to grant you what you can ask for in faith. She heals the sick, purges crimes, gladdens sorrowful hearts with holy exultation, calms sadness, smooths rough things, puts to flight the phantoms of demons. As ice is dissolved by fire, so by the merits of the most holy mother Anne the ancient enemy flees in confusion. Anne, ark of piety, drives away disgrace, preserves a fair reputation, and wondrously removes shameful love from the minds of her faithful.

Therefore honor Anne, you who pass through the toilsome life of this world. Anne obtains pardon for sinners, roots out vices, plants virtues. Anne cures diseases, heals wounds, drives out pestilence. Honor this mother, then, O children, for she is powerful to bring you into the sight of God. Whoever has her as advocate before God will fear no adversities of this world.

Therefore whoever desires to lead a tranquil and holy life on earth, whoever earnestly seeks forgiveness for his sins, let him never depart from the service of this most holy mother. For she rewards her devotees in many ways even in this life, and prepares eternal gifts for those who persevere. I was young and now am [unclear].
