Of Conrad Celtis Protucius, poet laureate: a tetrastich on Saint Anne.

Anne has never dismissed anyone’s prayers empty, but, radiant, has always brought the hoped-for aid. Therefore let us heap manifold honor upon the pious mother, who permits no one’s prayers to be empty.
Of Theodoricus Gresemundus the Younger of Mainz: a tetrastich to Saint Anne.
Anne, parent of the Virgin Mary, hail, favorable one, worthy [unclear] the work of our salvation. The human redemption which began through you, I pray, continue, covering our crimes with prayers.
Of Rodolphus Langius, canon of Münster: a distich on Saint Anne.
Great parent Anne, hear the vows which pregnant women, with fruitful womb, bring to you.
Of Jodocus Badius of Ghent: a tetrastich on Saint Anne.

Anne, glory of the world, mother of the mother of Jesus, by the merits of the mother, may your grandson grant the stars. Saint Anne, bringing forth the first-fruits of our salvation, help us with your offspring and with your grandson.
Rodolphus Agricola in his poem on Saint Anne, among other things, thus:

Anne, venerable mother of the mother of the highest Parent, you who first open the path of salvation to the peoples: from you flee all diseases, pallor and pain, and every harmful thing that dwells in soul or body; whatever there is among human beings that troubles cares and hearts flees from you, as clouds driven by winds are wont to do.
Rutgerus [venerable?], regular canon of [Baynen?], to the image of Saint Anne

Here with deep prayers and with devoted [unclear] I weep, where Anne, the parent, sits with her blessed offspring. Do not doubt: you will receive whatever you ask of him, for powerful Anne continually sends [it] by her prayers.
A distich by the same on Saint Anne
Anne, mother of the parent of Jesus Christ the mother of God, we ask of you: drive every sin away from us.
The rosary of Saint Anne by Jodocus [Beiffel?], patrician of Aachen, to the reverend father and lord, lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict.

Whoever wishes to read this rosary in honor of the most blessed mother Anne with devotion should recite the Lord's Prayer together with the salutation of Saint Anne, which he should repeat after every two verses; that salutation is as follows.

Hail, venerable Anne, mother of the Mother of God, most pleasing to the Holy Trinity, honored above all women, blessed are you by the Lord, and blessed is the fruit of your womb; and blessed is the blood born from you, Jesus Christ. Amen.
Our Father. Hail, [Mother] of God.

Anne, let me, wretched as I am, set forth your praises; for, if you permit, I shall bring you garlands and roses. Anne, you shine, a venerable offspring of the kings of Judah, renowned for your [unclear], with your pious husband Joachim. Anne, [unclear] you wept in your husband for chaste loves, the sole glory of married women and [unclear] honor. Anne, you seek a pious child, and not for vain uses, but that with holy posterity she may worship God. Anne, a swift messenger from the heavenly court announces to you: "Rejoice," he says, "for, exulting mother, you shall have offspring." Anne, you will bring forth offspring blessed with such great virtue that, with virginal honor, she will shine as Mother.
Hail.

Anne, you will bear a daughter whose [unclear], whom the world does not contain, God himself willingly enters your chaste womb. Anne, at last from your blood will arise the blood which, shed for the wretched, hopes [unclear] the guilty. Anne, so great an expectation befitted your childbirth, for it is no easy thing to have the mother of the Mother of God. Anne, the praises of your offspring will fly above the stars; all ages will proclaim you also blessed.
Our Father. Hail, [Mother] of God.

Anne, you are believed to have conceived Mary pure from evil, and to have had her holy before God. Anne, you bear things other than those which figures had signified, her whom the holy fathers sang would come. Anne, you bear the enclosed paradise, the tree of life, blessed and sacred with every honor of the countryside. Anne, heavily laden you bear the garden which the fiery [unclear] cherub guards, glowing night and day. Anne, you bear the flower that surpasses white lilies, humble violets, and the scarlet rose. Anne, in you the Mosaic ark is discerned, and the golden urn of heavenly bread lies there. Anne, you bear the bride of the true Solomon, and a house adorned within and without with every jewel. Anne, you bear the temple whose inner chambers sweet sounds, music, and every rejoicing have filled. Anne, you bear the veil, in the beautiful image of the fathers, holding within itself the things done, which may cover the ark of God. Anne, you bear the offspring whose head the golden flame of Phoebus clothes, and the white moon her snowy feet.
Our Father. Hail, [Mother] of God.

Anne, now made possessor of longed-for Mary, you can scarcely contain in your whole breast the joys that have arisen. Anne, all the stars applauded Mary newly born, and an unaccustomed radiance flowed from the pole. Anne, it is right to believe that angelic choirs celebrated the birthday of your child around you. Anne, the deep shades felt your childbirth; then the new light itself terrified the Stygian pools. Anne, as parent, you hesitate to touch your daughter with your hands, she who is brighter than the sun and than the lights of heaven. Anne, why do you fear to handle the heavenly girl? She smiles at her mother; she does nothing sad.
Hail.

Anna, [unclear], behold, your daughter reaches for the milky breasts, and seeks your neck with tender hands. Anna, you break off delays, baring breasts and bosom; you receive her tender little limbs in your tender lap. Anna, you cherish your daughter, and from your breast she draws the sweet juices with rosy mouth, sounding gracious murmurs. Anna, if you knew how great pains your daughter will bear, and how many deaths she will endure, you would now be nothing. Our Father. Hail, [unclear] of God. Anna, it is dear to your heart to adorn your daughter with approved morals, and to have ordered her for the highest God. Anna, you prepare to bring your daughter into the lofty shrine; but the nourishing one of her own accord reached the step of the heavenly ones. Anna, with slow pace and labor you follow the swift one. The eager little virgin consoles her weary mother. Anna, why do you marvel at strength in the tender virgin? You do not see human things, but holy signs of God. Anna, you are accustomed in poverty to give offerings to the sacred temples; now you give that than which no woman ever gave more. Anna, when you wished your consecrated daughter to dwell, she gladly entered the cloisters and [unclear] virginal Lord. Anna, about to send away the holy one, you wear away cheeks and eyes with weeping; deep love holds you unmoved. Anna, return home; leave your daughter trying [unclear]; unless she thinks of the one who is to come, “I am here.” Anna, may your daughter fly through the ethereal recesses; may love sent from the highest summit possess her. Anna, two Marys born to you are there to serve you; nor will they honor you with slight devotion. Our Father. Hail, [unclear] of God. Anna, by your weeping you have been taught to succor [unclear]. Hence also, when called by the wretched, you readily favor them. Anna, you are accustomed to overturn the fixed laws of nature, and so you will. Let the barren woman now be a joyful parent. Anna, you even set in place the gifts of flowing fortune, lest, slipping suddenly, they flee from our laps. Anna, you drive away disgrace; you give the gifts of fair fame. You relieve sorrows, and love yields to you. Anna, whether hostile force terrifies someone, or whether the bonds of a dark prison hold him, Anna, be present as faithful relief to sick mortals; with you as guide, lost life returns to the languishing. Anna, mother, the sailor calls upon you amid the fearful wave, if wind and water have laid the torn ship low. Anna, mother, you are always to be feared by the black tyrant; as ice flees fire, so that harmful one flees you. Anna, mortal hearts cannot ask of you in vain whatever you will, and whatever your daughter and God will. Anna, therefore blessed by merits and by so great offspring, Anna, great mother, look upon our prayers. Hail.

Prayer to be said after the rosary. Almighty and most merciful God, who deigned to choose blessed Anne as the mother of the mother of your Son: grant, we beseech you, that we who honor her memory with faithful devotion may, through her merits, obtain also the helps of eternal life. Through [etc.]

Here ends the rosary of Jodocus Beissel, professor of both laws, patrician of Aachen, addressed to the reverend father Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict. From Aachen, on the third day before the Ides of April, in the year 1483.
A poem of Adam Werner of Themar on the most holy Anne, addressed to the reverend father lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot.

Let us sing praises to the renowned grandmother. Dear kinsman of Jesus, move the plectra of praise; nor may you, chaste mother, daughter, be absent from the choir as I sing. Anne, offspring of kings, long endures barren in a second marriage, and grieves that she is without child. Weeping, she prays for offspring, nor do tears flow in vain. Heavenly messengers promise a child; pregnant, joined to her husband, then as childbearing mother she is approved by the birth, through whom our salvation came. Thus the venerable stock of Jesse grew green; the rod will be fruitful with fertile shoot; refreshed by its flower, we revive from the death pronounced upon us. By this birth Joachim becomes worthy to stand in the shrines, removing the reproaches of the priest. Thus, Anne, make us worthy to bear pure prayers to your grandson. Commend us to the boy whom holy charity bears; we ask it by prayer, O blessed matron. Christ denies you nothing. To Christ, who as companion of the Spirit reigns with the Father, be glory through all ages; whom your prayers, O Anne, grant as reconciled to us. Amen.

This hymn is sung under the melody of that hymn which, on the Nativity of Saint Mary, is used in many churches and begins: “Rejoice, mother, in your inmost bowels.” From the castle of Heidelberg, on the second day before the Kalends of February, 1494.
Johannes Herbst of Lauterburg, poem or hymn concerning Saint Anne, addressed to the reverend father lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot,
Rejoice, Anne, you who are a refuge for the wretched; we pray, we sing, we bring forth songs. On the holy feast, be present with your offspring; now we speak praises to you.
Rejoice, earth shining, fertile with grass and wet, drenched with deifying dew, from whom was born the Virgin, purer than the ether, innocent of sin.
Rejoice, you who had been of royal seed, already [unclear], given to a husband; you had led a chaste marriage, long without offspring, made a mother by a vow.

Rejoice, you who, at the reproach of the priest, [unclear], were confounded; with tears you call upon God. Having been heard, you receive your husband as he comes to meet you at the gate called Golden.
Rejoice, you who joyfully embraced Joachim, your husband, as he came to meet you; and, taught by a heavenly divine power, thus the Mother is conceived in your womb.
Rejoice, sagacious simplicity, praised by an angelic choir, and divided threefold: goods for the temple, for the needy and the poor, and a part for your servants.
Rejoice; the people of the faithful celebrates the feast. [unclear]; and by your prayers, Anne, may you render Christ propitious. Amen.

This hymn takes the melody of that hymn which is sung concerning the Ascension of the Lord, namely Festum nunc celebre, etc., and of that hymn concerning the martyrs, Sanctorum merita inclita, etc. From Heidelberg, February 3, 1494.
An elegiac poem of Mutgerus, venerable regular canon in Heyna, in the diocese of Worms, on Saint Anne.
Of the splendor of the fatherland, of the brightness of uncreated light, splendid mother of the Virgin Mother, hail.
You, holy one, bore for the Lord a divine maiden, from whom Jesus, the kindly light of the world, came forth.
You, Anne, steadfastly call the one born your grandson, although he himself made the heavens and the ground.
In the flesh Jesus himself is your grandson; he joined supreme divinity to flesh, for he is God and man.
Therefore, although Jesus has always existed, yet he chooses and deigns to be called your grandson.
Do not hesitate to assail such a grandson with prayers, Anne; we ask you, who will carry all things asked.
If at first he has not bent ready ears, run more swiftly, Anne, to your daughter.
Let your daughter show her breasts to her son Christ; straightway the kindly parent will grant what is desired.
If the matter is very difficult to obtain by prayer, let the daughter seek help with her mother.
My faith is firm, and I do not doubt that presently the Lord will hear both as they pray with a gracious ear.
Therefore, brothers, with continual prayers one ought to seek the help of Anne and Mary together.
It is established that if you honor the mother of the Lord's mother, [unclear] you cultivate the very title of the Virgin Mother.
Again, if you venerate the mother of the Lord, it is clear [unclear] that you prepare praises to the Lord in the mother.
May praise, power, and honor be to the Son born from Anne's child, and to the highest Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.
A Sapphic poem of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, on the day of Saint Anne.
Let us celebrate the feasts of sacred Anne, of the mother excellent in merits, who brought forth to the world the mother of the Son of God the Father.
Her venerable [unclear] life is deservedly praised by us: blessed, distinguished by endowment, bringing relief to wretched minds.
She heals the weak, purges all evils, brightens the hearts of the sorrowful with joy, sets fitting things before us, directs and governs, smooths rough things.
Mighty, residing in the court of the highest King, she wipes away stains by prayer, bestows grace, and leads faithful souls to the stars.
Famous mother, help, preserve, refresh, and govern the brothers here who frequent your feasts, uttering vows and praying to you for good things.
May honor and power be to the Thunderer above, who, God simple and likewise triune, has bestowed the crown of great glory upon Anne forever. Amen.

This Sapphic hymn is sung to the melody of Ut queant laxis, Vita sanctorum, Virginis proles, Quod chorus vatum, Iste confessor, and similar hymns that are Sapphic in their song. From Sponheim, July 7, 1497.
An elegiac poem of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, on holy mother Anne.
How great the rewards that Anne gives to her devotees, no one grasps in mind nor can speak with mouth.
She drives harsh things away, obtains pardon, increases the adornments of honor for her own, and causes them to be in heaven.
By contrast, many exceedingly bitter things accompany those who despise mother Anne; take heed beforehand for yourself.
She [crushes?] the proud, casts the powerful down from honor, and [allows?] them often to endure great scandals.
This is clear and remains fixed: Anne offers joyful things to those who honor her, but, grim, brings back many things to her enemies.
Therefore, men, I advise you: serve so great a patroness; let the female choir also be present together in love.
What we write is clearly established by examples; open ears will receive what helps devout hearts.
From Sponheim, July 17, 1493.
A Sapphic poem of Rutger the Sicambrian, for a hymn in praise of Saint Anne.
We sing your praises, venerable Anne; favor those who praise you with their measures, obtaining for all the pardon of salvation, and granting rewards.
You, Anne, parent of the mother of Christ, shining in the highest citadel of [heaven?], obtain whatever you ask of the Begotten of the almighty one.
You heal the sick, wipe away stains, make your faithful servants attain their prayer, and at last grant them to climb into the heavenly kingdom.
By your approved character, Anne, you bent the highest Lord with many prayers, so that he would grant that you become the mother of so great an offspring in the world.
To the highest Father, to the heavenly Son, and to the Holy Spirit be honor and power, brightness, virtue, holiness, and [unclear] for all [time?].
Another by the same.
Anne, mother of the virgin mother, let us all resound diligent praises with all the powers of the inmost heart, with ringing voice.
She brought forth for the wretched race, stained by the blemish of mother Eve, the changing offspring, and the radiant beam which she gave to the world.
This light of the world, as it passed through the darkness, drove all things away, shining with heavenly light, as holy John resounds in the sacred book.
Anne, mother of the divine maiden, you call the groaning grandson [unclear]; do not refuse the people praying, so far as the flesh is concerned.
Virgin, on our behalf, favor the prayers of Anne, your mother, who earnestly entreats; you, grandson Jesus, easy to entreat, fulfill her prayer.
To the Son born of Anne’s daughter, with the highest God, be honor and power; to the blessed Spirit let equal honor be for all time.
A poem by the same, in iambic dimeter, which is sung to the melody of the Ambrosian hymns.
Bowed down, let us honor blessed Anne’s feast, singing due thanks with our voices and in our inmost hearts.
This mother of the gracious Virgin, who brought forth the radiance of the world; this woman who by her virtues made herself most pleasing to God.
She drives away delays; she confers grace by her prayers. She lightens most dreadful illnesses, of body as well as spirit.
In praise of her, King of heaven, to you with resounding songs, and at once to the [unclear] Spirit, we bring forth pious praises. Amen.
A poem in alcinamic meter by the same, which is sung to the melody “Crux fidelis” or “Pange lingua.”
This company, with voice, vows, and pious hearts, is eager to utter the feasts of Anne, so illustrious a mother. Be gentle, we pray, to those who praise you.
You, parent of Mary’s mother, you, most pleasing to God, preserved the beginnings of the law which Moses once gave to the ancient fathers and to the Hebrew peoples.
Wondrous gifts, gracious one, you obtain for the faithful by prayer pleasing to the Son of the high Father. You heal the sick, and grant that hearts be pure.
May the Father, and also the Son with the Spirit, entreat you; and may you, rejoicing, give to us as we sing praises of the renowned Anne, foremother of the kindly Virgin. Amen.
A poem of Rutger Venrai, a German, regular canon of Hein, on the book concerning the praises of Saint Anne.

Whoever you will be, reader of this excellent book, put vain fear aside; it contains nothing frivolous. Now pregnant with wondrous meaning, and sweet with charm, Abbot Trithemius has produced it by his art: watching over books, guardian of the Sponheim fold, who cultivates the sacred writings of threefold language. Here you will find titles of Anne full of reason and art; only turn them over with a pious heart. He does not follow vain and everywhere doubtful little tales; he teaches the clear streams of sacred eloquence. Therefore, I pray, read with love the worthy praises of venerable Anne, which the learned man has brought forth for you in love.
Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, greeting to the reader.

When recently, at the insistence of friends, I had resolved to write something about the praises of the most holy mother Anne, certain fathers of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel asked that I not omit the defense of Mary’s most pure conception. And so, moved by their prayers and otherwise persuaded by just reason, [unclear] the seventh chapter of this work, concerning the conception

I have set down beforehand [what concerns] the Mother of God and Virgin; and lest anyone receive it otherwise than my intention holds, I have thought that the readers should be warned. For I know, and it does not escape me, that many most holy and most learned men once wrote that the Mother of God was subject to the original stain, men who flourished long before the Council of Basel. Now I pass over their opinion, [unclear]; and I intend to say or write nothing at all against them. Indeed, if anyone sees that some things have been said by me rather harshly, let him refer them not to those who hold opinions otherwise than we do, but only to the points [unclear], which, without learning, the babblers who assert another opinion do not fear to call heretical. And this is what my [writing] indicates; it notes nothing further of the past. For when I say that whatever solid foundation [unclear] which the unskilled murmur, this belongs to what is further, not to what is past; and today it censures obstinate men, not the ancient contrary opinions.

But you ask what learned men have written to the contrary: I am not referring to the ancient Fathers, but I mean those who, after the determination of the Council of Basel, think otherwise. And so only the obstinacy of the more ignorant persons of this [unclear], not the learned inquiry of those who hold another opinion, is censured; indeed I am not ignorant of the declaration of Sixtus IV, Supreme Pontiff. But it has seemed to me that the most pure conception of [the Virgin] is in no way at variance with the faith of the holy Roman Church, which she believes and venerates, as she shows today by many documents. Finally, with the doctors of the universities of Paris, Cologne, Heidelberg, Erfurt, Vienna, Leipzig, Tübingen, Ingolstadt, Basel, Mainz, and many others at Rome and in nearly all the orders, with the Christian faithful spread throughout the whole Christian world, I am not afraid to venerate the pure conception of the Mother of God and Virgin Mary; I do not admit obstinacy, if, obedient to the Roman Church, I wish [to remain] in the reverence of that venerable Church, my nurse and mother. This is the pure and sincere intention of this chapter of mine, in which I think that no one’s opinion is in any respect diminished by me, briefly and without obstinacy. Reader, farewell.

This letter of the lord father Johannes, abbot, is missing from certain copies through carelessness and negligence; nevertheless he himself commands that it be appended to all copies, and has decreed that it be considered appended to each one.

Epistola domini iohannis tritemi abbatis Spanhemēsis in librum de laudibus sanctissime Anne Enerabili religiosissimoqz patri. dio Rumuldo laupach Priori convento Franckfordensis.ordis frarri beate marie semp viginis de monte carmel Johannes de tritenhem abbas monasterij sancti Martini in spanhem ordinis divi patris benedicti. salutē et charitātē. Voto nostro et tuis peticōibet(optime pater) satisfacere cupientes: libri de laudibet sanctissime matris an ne sincera deuotōe colōcripsimet: quē tuo nomini dicamet: quoniā ante alios nobis dignus visus es: vt pote cultor maximet amator q̄ deuotissimet eiusde venerabilis anne De-historia vero que satē Vulgata est nihil aut parū assumptimet:quia nobis et minus pro bata visa est: et in plerisqz locis apocrifa. Meqz tamē redarguē illaz voluimet: ne simplicibus occasionē pberemus murinurādi: si (vt ipsi estimāt) antiquitate pbatam noua plumpōe carpere mus. Dimisimet ergo intacta historia et que aptissima.fide. veri cāte ac ratione nota fuerat ex dono dei ad honorem sancte matris anne contulimet. Miracula quōqz sancte anne ab hoc volumine reiecumet: ne viris eruditis (qui bis nō facile adhibēt fidem) tra ccatum nostrum suspectū redderemet. Alio itaqz tpe si voles de illis texetur historia. In quibusculqz te hesitare contigerit.rescri be: priōptos inuenies nos qui tibi et omnibus de singulis que scri psūnus rationē demōstremet. Post finē huius operis qdā carmio de laudibet sancte matris aduiximet:q nobis a diversis eruditi vi ris sune transmissa. Vale. Ex spanhem kalendis Iulias. Anno dni M,cccc,xciiiij.

Incipit tractatus domini Johannis tritemij abbatis spanhemensis. ordinis scti benedicti: de laudibus venerabilis et beatissime matris dei genitricis Anne.
Oti cōpellit necessicas. et mentis purget devotio vt laudes beatissime matris dei genitricis Anne pro viribet ingenij ad edificatione fideliũ scribā: et quanta miseris pietate subuenire consueuerit.
Veraci narratione denunciez. Sed cui paupratem ingenij mei considerero : impurus de sanctissima loqui ptimesco.
Quanta em laude digna sit. que dei genitricem peperit. quis sermo explicabit: Volo itaç aliquid ad honorē tāte matris cudere et timeo: qu quicquid dixero landibet eiet minet est: quicqḍ scripsero rei maiestate pcul inferius est Eniuero cu illius in miseris beneficiā ad memoria revoco: tacere a landibus eins etiā si volo non posstuz. Minc pietas maxima votũ promervuit: deuotionem excitasit:requirit honoris exhibitione. Deuota quoç(ne dicaz importuna)peticio amicoy me non minus vt auderē impulit: de quoy fide et oione nostra infirmitas fiducia acceptit. Quamuis igitur me peccatoře nouerim: quāuis regine celi sanctissima parrentem dignē laudare nō sufficiā: nequaç tamena pposito laudis debeo recedere: ne ingratisudinis vicium videar incurrisse.
Conabor pro deuotione mea q̄ valeo: q̄ nemo quod nō potet. a deo exigitur. nemo apud ineternũ indicem bone volūtatis vascuus indicatuer. Laudabo igitur hō des: famulus dnāz: peccator sanctissimā. Meq̄ eni a laude dei peccatores cohibuit: q̄ in psalmo dixit. Laudate dũm omies gentes: laudate euz omies populi Enimuero dum gentes ad laudē dni excitat. quid alind quā pec catores vocat: Erant ein longe a iusticia: quia non deũ. sed ydola colebât. Nemo ergo tacere a laudibus dei pmittitur: quādo etiā gentes ydolatre ad penitentiam vocātur. Laudent ergo dominũ omies qui misericordiā eius pecipiunt: laudāt omies qui in carne vivunt: quia ipse est qui omes nos condidit: ipse qui vitaz decit. laudet iustet simul et peccator: ille q̄ misericordia dñi ne caderet servatus est: iste quia etiā post lapsum ne ineternũ periret ereceet Eti si non sit speciosa laus in ore peccatoris. nemine tamen a laudibus dei excusat rea conscientia: cu ad penitentiam eins miseris cordia omes reservuentur. Ferat iustus laudem: peccator pfeissio nez. Laudet ille quoniā gratia presevante fortiter stetit: pfiteaç iste q̄ misericordia subsequēte surrexit. Lauda aia mea dominũ: laudabo deiũ meu in vita meu: psallaz dño quadiu fuero. Aperia os meum ad confitendũ dño: mentez pariter aptabo et calamũ:

laudes beatissime matris anne qua possumi devotione cantabo.
Nam si deum generaliter in sanctis suis laudare precipimur: parentes eius sine dubio specialius honorare persuademur. Qui enim nobis parentes nostros honorare precepit: suos scōm carnē minime excludit. Sancti ergo est fratres charifissimi sedulas ilo lis devotionis laudes impendere: de quō. sanguine carnem dei filii credimus sumpsisse Inter quos beatissima dei genitrix iure obtinet principatū: cuius tanta sunt merita sanctitatis: ut super choras angeloy exaltata sit in celis. Post es sanctissima illi? ma ter anna de qua loqui instituim? sicut carne dei filio est prīa: ita vitū meritis p sanctis ceteris credit accepta Mec de sanctitate eius nobis licet dubitare: qua sine originālis culpe macula dei matrē credimus peperisse. Non enim potuit tante virginis mater esse nisi sancta: per cui? partū virginei. sumpsimus eterne salu tis remedia. Anna radix sancta: maria virgo arbor sanctissima fructus dei filius animay medicina. Arbor bons. arbor sancta: arbor sine huana cultura secundissima: que de sancta radice sūp sit exordiū: de pinguedine celestis pluuiie incrementū. Nunquaz bona radix malā arborē procreat: nūcī malos fructus arbor bo no portat. qui non sum dignus faciem meam levare ad celos. pre multitudine iniquitatis meae quantominus annee beatissime laudes imputis labris audiam contingere. Gratia autem tua sum id quod sum: et totus quod boni volo et possum. Tu enim domine voluitatem vt bona velit et bona sit. per gratiam tuam illuminas: tu etiam es qui nobis operari pro bona voluntate prestatas. In oib voluntatem nostram prevenientem gratiam tuam agnoscimus tua in bonis que volumus et facimus: sine nostris meritis nona predicamus. Nihil a nobis nisi malum: nihil a te prouenit nisi bonum. Cum ergo nihil possim boni a memetipso sine gratia tua: ad te devotus consugio: te humili subiectione interpellor: vt quod merita mea ppediunt: gratie tuo clemens largiar Da mihi domine secum tuorum affricem sapientiam: vt me cum sit, et mecum laboret omni tempore. et in hoc potissimum ope in quo exignis viribus nomen tuum in sancta mater anna laudare constitui. Tu etiam anna mater sanctissima de cuius memoria agis. tu mihi solita benignitate adesse digneris: vt ad laudes tuas describendas idoneus efficiar: et meritis suis terophantes fidelis inueniar. Domina mea, spes mea, aduocata mea, in omni tribulatione: laudare te cupienti nunc clemens adesto: et que voluntatem ad scribendum multiplici beneficio prouocasti: impetra meritis tuis facultate ingenio pauperi, vt digna te laudare sufficiat. Nihil nisi trium honorum quero: nihil nisi tibi complacere desidero: non nisi recta et vera de tuis laudibus scribere intendo. Nunc ovo fer opeim: da manu auxili: impetra gratia. Tu etiam dei genitrix immaculata, que annam venerabile matre tuae famulos tuos honorare docuisti. adesto mihi laudes et describere cupienti meritis tuis: vt devotio famuli tui debitum sorciat effusa ctus in opere: quem gratia dei concepit in mente. Dus quocce leste patrie beati spis qui in sacratissimo matris et filie virginis fructu domino nostro biesu christo exultatis: vestris orationibus dignum me anna laudatorum reddite: et sanctispiritus gratiam mibi impetrate. Si matrem et filiam in celesti gaudio colitis: dignum est vt laudatoribus earum in hac peregrinatione assistatis. Nos etiam beatissime anna denoti cultores nostris pijs studijs nolite detrabere: sed si in aliquibus ex infirmitate defecimus per charitatem exculcate. Nihil per contentionem sine inanem gloria a me scribitur: Nihil a pocripbe dubietatis allegatur: nihil nisi probatum assumitur. Nihil recipio quod divinis inaucturis obnuer: Nihil scribo quod fidem christians maculet: nis nihil introduco quod fancis non concordet

Mon ergo mihi doctior te anna laudasti detrahat: no mibi equa lis deroget: non mibi inferior insulceret. Vincie quod veru est: nec deficit quod a vero procedit. Memo me de sanctissima scribente ppter me contemnendum existimet: nemo devotione meaz con vexet: nemo contra laudes dnie matriis anna susturret. Canum la tratus non metuo: imperito censures non timeo: invidia faces non horresco. Scribo emi devotionis non improbis: studiosis non ignaris: builibus no superbis. Placeat illis presens opus quib scribitur: proficiat quibus offerit: conducat quibus exhibet. Omid mihi de bis q foris sunt: Quid ad me qui non recta sapiunt: Quid mihi de sancta preter rationem corrodunt: Illis dislicere non timeo: quorum censuras et iudicia temeraria cognosco.

Si sumo gubernatoris Deo vultis complacere credite mihi fratres, quoniam vera dicturus sum: si venerabilem matrem ex toto corde diligitis et colitis: quantu ei deferat celestis imperator experientia cognoscetis. Tante apud deum potestat est: ut quicquid ab eo pecierit: sine mora valeat obtinere. Affime matris anne cum multa reverentia populi quiescet: quam sanctus longinus miles christi primus fundasse dicitur. et pio etissimas illas reliquias ab hyerusalem secundum deferens in eadem collocasse Muius rei in dicto cenobio antiquissima monumenta reperiuntur. Ista ne tibi nova videntur: Cessa igitur festo sanctissime matris detrahere: cessa cultus eius dignissimi impio dete lacerare. Moli odius psionale diffundere in omnes: noli propter paucos displicentis oibus indignari: noli iniuriam homis effero re in superos. Cur lesus (forte ab hoie) sanctos dei vocas in culam? Cessa obsecro cessa vindictam unius homis vel paucorum sanctissima matre anna velle exigere. Molo sanctitatem ei via superes: nolo eaz suo honore prines: nolo devotione servor eam impugnes. Si peccauerit ho in homine. placare poterit ei deus: qui aut peccat in sanctos dei imparentes filii dei. in matrem generatrix dei: quis orabit pro eo? Quo potest deu habere epicum: qui sanctos eius et quidem sanctissimos habet offensos: Sancta anna omni honore digna est: que parere meruit dei genetricem sine labe criminis: cui honorum qui minuit: iniuriam deo facit. Quin poti si sapis. si intelligis. recede ab hac stulticia tua: fuge ab hac insania falsa: declina ab hac blasphemia pessima: et pristini erroris assume penitentiam: et per compuctionis lachrymas et nchphariam diluas culpam. Quod si no feceris: si in prinacia tua perseveraueris: non impedies voluntate dei: sed partem habebis in sorte dyaboli. Deus sancta anna in ecclesia sua honorare disposuit: quis euz prohibebit: Ecce reges et principes memoria sancte annae religiosa devotione concelebrant: ecce presules ecclesiar vbicq in eius honorez altaria consecrant: ecce fideles populi nomen eius vbicq inuocant: et tu in invidia tua cui dyabo bolo tabescis. prunderis et insanis. Monachi et religiosi utriusq sexus totus ecclesiar dei clerus. festum sancte matris annae et memoria cum singulari devotione celebrant: et tu inuide canis contra omnes latrare presumis: Quid impie latras: quid scelet rate murmurass: Tace abi. recede: non sine graui animaduersione bec tua impietas vindicabitur. Quicunge in honori sanctitati beatissime matris annae detraxerit: quicunge cultores eius blasphemauerit: sine confusione ab hac vita non migrabit. Dei paraetis et virginis praenotavi: quae ne quisquae aliter quam mea habeat intentio suscipiat: lectorum putavi admonédi. Novi enim nec me fugit quae multae sanctissimi atque doctissimi viri olim de genetricem subiacuisse originali macule scripsérunt: qui longe ante basilienne concilium claruerunt. Nunc ego sententiam tibi coecedes penitentiam pertráseo: nihilquae olim praeterea dicé vel scribē intendo. Enim vero si quae me durius dictae cernit: nō in opiniones aliter quam nos. Sed in punctis duaexat referat: quae sine eruditione garritaes aliter opinionis assertores appellare hereticos nō verent. Et hoc ubi mea insinuat: quae praeterea nō pteriti notat. Quod enim dico quid solidi lacraet. quae imperiti murmurât: praeterea est: nō pteriti: et hodie praenaces arguit nō antiquae aliter opiniones. Interrogas vero quae eruditus vngi coetrarii scripsérunt: nō de antiquis patribus infero. Sed de his quae post determinationem patris coecilii aliter opinionatur intendó. Itaque solae praenacia quaerudae imperitior huius episcopoe nō opinionis eruditoe quaerudae aliter sentiuntur arguunt: quippe qui sivei quarti pontificis maximi declarationem nō ignoro. Mihi aut visu est a sancta romana ecclesia nulleton abhorreere purissime coeceptioes fidè: quam illa credit et venerat: quod hodie multae documêtis ostèdit. Denique cum doctoribus gymnasioe, patrisensis coloniensis, heyldebergen, erfordensis, wenensis, liptzoesis, thowingensis, engolstatensis, basiliensis, maguittenensis, alios rumaes multae et alibus pene ordinibus, christioe fidelibus per universum orbem christianum diffusis, receptione de genetricis et virginis marie purae venerari nō timéo: praenacioe nō admitto: si romae ecclesia obediens in obae et matris reverèdissime olim ecclesiae volo. Hec patris capitoe mei purae et sincera intentio est: in quo nullis suis brevi et sine praenacia opinionis derogati existimo. Lector vale.
